Written by the party that acted. Append-only: an entry is never edited or removed. Not a term.
The seller states it from data the buyer can't recompute. Not a term, and it changes without a new version.

Each line item lands in the one that the `transaction_mechanism` in effect (§ 5.9) maps to:
A line item agreed under a deal mechanism (§ 5.9) becomes a Deals API 1.0 `Deal`.
The system named by `deal_origin` (§ 5.9) pushes the `Deal` to the DSP named by `buyer_requirements.seats.dsp`.
The `Deal` takes these values from the agreed line item:
`commitment.flight.end` and `terms.enddate` are the flight's last second, inclusive.
The Deals API 1.0 doesn't say whether `enddate` is inclusive, so this mapping states it.
`terms.dealfloor` and `Deal.bidfloor` are prices per thousand impressions, so this table maps a `CPM` entry.
A `GeoCode` (§ 5.5) converts for the OpenRTB 2.6 `Geo` object: `country` takes the ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 code of the country, and `region` takes the part of an ISO 3166-2 code after the hyphen.
`terms.countries` takes the same alpha-3 code.
The list names whole countries, so `US` minus `US-TX` sends `USA`, and `geo` in the agreed record holds the exclusion.
The record holds no country for an extension term, so the system that pushes the `Deal` supplies the one the term lies in.
The line item's `status` ends at `agreed` (§ 5.1).
After the push, the deal's state is the Deals API `sellerstatus` and, for each seat, `BuyerStatus.status`.
A `direct_io` line item that books in OpenDirect 2.1, and the reservation of a `programmatic_guaranteed` line item, become a `Line` in an `Order`.
OpenDirect says who acts: on the seller's OpenDirect server, the buyer adds the `Order` to its `Account`, adds the `Line`, and reserves or books it.
The `Order` and `Line` take these values from the agreed line item:
Any other `cost_method`, and `TIME` with another `rate_unit`, has no `ratetype` and no mapping here.
A `direct_io` line item under one books in another order system, which its `order` entry names (§ 5.10), and changes there.
OpenDirect's cap counts a unique user, so it has no key for `frequency_cap.per`.

The record holds no value for `Order.name` and `Line.name`, or for `Order.accountid`, `Order.publisherid`, `Order.advertiserbrandid`, and `Line.productid`, which name the server's own `Account`, `Organization`, `AdvertiserBrand`, and `Product` resources.
OpenDirect 2.1 has the buyer obtain those ids from the publisher and its server, and no key here says which `Product` a line item books.
The ids of the `Order` and the `Line` go in `external_references[]`, and the `Line`'s state is its `bookingstatus`.

It is also normative for the lifecycle of the object to its terminal statuses, and for what a section of this document says a request or response carries, such as `errors[]` (§ 2.4), an `AvailabilityRead` (§ 3.3), and a `Commit` and its `CommitResult` (§ 5.6.1).

It is not normative for replay semantics beyond the rule in § 5.6.1, for any lifecycle after `agreed`, or for how a message states the buyer's `Party`, the form of a brief, or how an issued proposal reaches the buyer.
The nearest artifact is the pre-release `iab-agentic-primitives` library, version 0.5.1.
Those messages carry no proposal, `Commit`, or `errors[]`, so they are a model for the binding, not the binding itself.
A message signature proves an `https` origin.
An `assent[]` entry travels in the body of a signed message, as optional evidence, and § 4.1.2 states when the signature attributes it to a party.
After `agreed`.

`Object` holds keys that another definition sets.
A lead-in that reads "`X` holds the keys of `Y`" gives `X` every key of `Y`, with the rules `Y` states on them, and the rows of its own table.
The keys sit flat in `X`, and `X` doesn't repeat them.
`Y` may take a type, such as `Range[T]`.
A lead-in that adds "each `<marker>`" gives the composed keys that marker.
A lead-in that reads "`X` lists these paths" is followed by a `text` block with one path per line.
The first segment of a path is a key of `X`, and later segments nest as they do in the object `X` is a subset of.
A segment written `<name>` stands for what the lead-in says.
A key table led in by "`X` adds this key" or "`X` adds these keys" follows that block and gives `X` those keys beside the listed paths.
A list is written once, as ``a` \| `b``, or ``a`` alone when it has one value, or as the first column of a value table the text names as the list.

Agents that can spend read this object, and much of it is text the counterparty wrote: `description`, `media_kit_detail`, `best_for[]`, `not_suitable_for[]`, `seasonality_notes`, `approval`, `creative_policy`, `ext` values, a `FormatSpec`'s `spec`, a change request's `comments`, an error's `detail`, and the document behind a `DocumentRef`.
